about.title: About the atlas
about.what: The Plectis Atlas is an independent guide to OpenAI’s mathematics release of {release_date}. It follows the release’s grouping of its papers into {families} families, sets the Lean statements of {families_with_lean} of them beside the paper theorems they are paired with, gives each paper a reading page, and records who has checked what.
about.approach_intro: In August and September 2026, mathematicians wrote about what AI-generated results ask of the people who read them. These essays shaped how the atlas is built. Their authors have not reviewed the atlas and are not involved in it.
about.approach_response_intro: What the atlas does about it:
approach_responses: Each family page opens with the claim as the paper prints it, with its hypotheses and its place in the paper, and every paper has a reading page.
Where the release has a Lean statement, it sits beside the paper’s theorem, with outside readings of whether it states all of it. Neither stands in for the other.
The atlas counts what has been checked and by whom, and credits each kind of work where it appears.
Each paper’s references are listed, earlier work can be credited at the passage it bears on, and every outside check carries its author, date and source.
Every family is open for an explanation, a check or a correction, credited by name and made with or without an AI assistant.

approach_items.title: The technical debt of AI-generated mathematics
approach_items.argues: argues that a correct result nobody can follow leaves a debt for other mathematicians to pay, and that whoever publicises such work should make it understandable.

approach_items.who: Silvia De Toffoli and Eamon Duede
approach_items.title: After Math
approach_items.argues: separate a valid answer, which a formal certificate can establish, from an intelligible solution that mathematicians can grasp, communicate and build on.

approach_items.title: Deep theorems were scarce and difficult
approach_items.argues: argues that theorem counts no longer show understanding, and asks that discovery, proof, formalisation and explanation each be credited.

approach_items.title: If math is more than proof
approach_items.argues: asks that motivated explanations, which show why a result is true and why it was worth asking, earn the credit that proofs do.

approach_items.who: A declaration posted by Terence Tao and first signed by 25 Fields Medallists
approach_items.title: A Severe Misalignment of AI in mathematics
approach_items.argues: warns that rushing AI systems at famous problems puts attribution and the human transmission of ideas at risk.

approach_items.title: A beginning for mathematics
approach_items.argues: argues that mathematics should be judged by human understanding, which makes the people who explain and teach it more necessary.

about.adds_heading: What the atlas adds to the release
about.adds_intro: OpenAI’s release publishes {manuscripts} current papers as PDF and TeX, {lean} Lean challenge files with their configurations, a catalogue, and notes on what the Lean covers. For each of its {families} families, the atlas adds:
adds_items: a reading page for every paper, with each formula typeset and each theorem anchored; a page that did not convert in full lists what is missing, and the PDF stays the reference;
the main theorems, located and numbered as printed, each linked to its passage;
each Lean statement beside the paper theorem it is paired with, with the evidence for the pairing said at the join, and marked as a candidate until a person reviews it;
re-runs of OpenAI’s Lean solutions reported by outside groups, each credited and dated, at the release’s pinned commit;
outside readings of whether each family’s Lean statements state its headline, each in the reader’s own terms;
checks in a second proof assistant and by exact computation, where outside groups have made them;
the citations between the release’s papers, in both directions;
a way to explain, check or correct any of it, credited by name.
about.backend: Every evidence state on the site, every pairing of a paper theorem with a Lean statement and every number comes from Statement Map, a backend by Will Cook that joins the release’s statements, Lean challenges, outside readings and contributions into records pinned to the release, with a receipt behind every count. The site renders its decisions and makes none of its own.
about.backend_pin: This build reads one pinned export of it: generation {generation} of reader schema {schema}, exported by {exporter} from Statement Map commit {commit}, whose acceptance receipt ({receipt}) records the tests it passed at commit {runtime}. A page never mixes two generations; the build stops if any packet differs from the export.
about.independence_groups: It is equally independent of every group whose work it credits: {groups}. Each group’s findings are shown as their own, in their own terms, and none of them has reviewed or endorsed the atlas.
about.since_intro: Three pieces published since the release bear on how the atlas words what it shows.

since_items.title: What mathematicians should know about the Lean Theorem Prover: questions of reliability and AI
since_items.says: a guest post on Terence Tao’s blog (9 October 2026), explains that Lean’s kernel check is the core safeguard, and that a person must still confirm that a formal statement and its definitions say what was intended. This is why every Lean statement here is shown whole, with who compared it with the paper and what they found.

since_items.title: Changes to the Erdős problems web site
since_items.says: a guest post on Terence Tao’s blog (6 October 2026), describes removing problem statuses and the count of solved problems from erdosproblems.com, in favour of neutral wording such as “it is known that”, with a source. The atlas follows the same discipline: it says what is recorded and by whom, and keeps no tally of results.

since_items.title: AHM Statement on OpenAI’s October 6 Release of Mathematical Documents
since_items.says: reposted on Terence Tao’s blog (7 October 2026), sets out its view of the release and asks mathematicians to stop working with OpenAI. The atlas records it as one perspective on the release, and neither joins nor answers it.

about.since_note: None of these authors has reviewed or endorsed the atlas.
about.how: Scripts read the release at commit {commit_short} and extract catalogue entries, available manuscript sources, bibliographies, Comparator files and scope notes. The generated pages link back to the source files. Each paper’s reading page is converted from its TeX, with every formula checked by KaTeX; a page that did not convert in full lists what is missing, and the PDF stays the reference. Contribution status comes from the atlas’s own records.
about.independence: The atlas is an independent project. It is not affiliated with or endorsed by OpenAI. It describes what is in the release and what has been checked, and quotes OpenAI’s own words where it describes the results.
about.licence: The release is published by OpenAI under the Apache License 2.0. The atlas typesets selected descriptions, abstracts, statements and notes from the pinned release and links to their source files.
about.cite: Cite a page by its address and the pinned commit it describes.
about.author: {author} builds and maintains the atlas. His own work on Erdős problems, with its Lean proofs, is at Plectis.
about.made: Will Cook built the atlas with AI coding agents (Anthropic’s Claude) under his direction. The repository contains the scripts used to extract and count material from the pinned release. AI-made classifications, such as the scope of each Lean statement, are labelled as drafts and await human review. Named statement reviews and replay receipts are recorded separately.
about.not: The atlas records source material, review reports and replay receipts. It does not provide peer review or endorse the release’s results. Each page states which checks are recorded.

sources.lede: Everything on the atlas comes from {sources} sources: OpenAI’s repository, the atlas’s own checks, and public work by {people} other people, with {findings} of their findings attached to specific results.
sources.credit: Other people’s data and findings are folded into the atlas’s own rows and credited at every point of use. Code, data files and prose are copied only where the author’s licence allows; otherwise the atlas cites the finding and links the original.
sources.openai_uses: The catalogue, the {manuscripts} current manuscripts in {families} families with their TeX sources and bibliographies, the {lean} Comparator challenge files and the Lean library, OpenAI’s Lean notes and its history file.

The method follows Will Cook’s claim-faithful publication system for his Erdős problem corpus.
